"Kick something off" is a phrasal verb that means to start or begin something — usually an event, a project, a campaign, a meeting, a season, or any organized activity.

Think of it as a more energetic, vivid way of saying "begin" or "start."

"We kicked off the meeting with a short introduction."
→ We started the meeting with a short introduction.

"The festival kicks off on Friday."
→ The festival begins on Friday.
Where Does It Come From? (The Origin)

The idiom comes from sports — specifically football (both American football and soccer).

In these sports, a "kickoff" is the literal kick of the ball that starts the game. A player kicks the ball from the center of the field, and the moment that kick happens, everything begins. The game is alive.

Over time, people borrowed this image of a sharp, energetic kick launching something into motion, and started using it in everyday language for starting anything — not just games.

So when you say "let's kick off this meeting," you're painting a picture of launching it the same way a ball is launched at the start of a game — with energy and a clear sense of "this is where it all begins."

"Kick off" is a phrasal verb — a verb made of two parts (verb + particle). It can be used in two ways:

1. Transitive (with an object):
You kick something off. The object goes either in the middle or after "off."

"She kicked off the campaign with a big speech."
"She kicked the campaign off with a big speech." ✅ Both are correct.

2. Intransitive (without an object):
The thing itself kicks off — it starts on its own.

"The concert kicks off at 8 PM."
"The season kicked off last week."

The same idea becomes a noun when you write it as one word: kickoff (American English) or kick-off (British English).

"The kickoff of the new project is on Monday."
"What time is the kickoff?" (asking when something starts)
"We had a kickoff meeting to plan everything." (a meeting held at the very beginning of a project)

In business language, a "kickoff meeting" is very commonly used — it refers to the first official meeting that launches a project.
Tone and Register — When Do People Use It?

"Kick off" is informal to semi-formal. This means:

  • ✅ Perfect for everyday conversation
  • ✅ Very common in the workplace (business meetings, project management)
  • ✅ Common in sports commentary and news
  • ❌ Slightly too casual for formal written documents (where you'd say "commence," "launch," or "inaugurate" instead)

It carries a sense of energy, enthusiasm, and momentum — it makes the beginning of something sound exciting and deliberate, not dull.

In sports:

"The World Cup kicks off next month."
"The referee blew the whistle, and the match kicked off."

In business / work:

"Let's kick off today's meeting by reviewing last week's goals."
"The company kicked off its new marketing campaign in January."

In entertainment:

"The band kicked off their world tour in London."
"The new season kicks off with a dramatic two-part episode."

In everyday life:

"They kicked off the celebrations with fireworks."
"She kicked off the day with a 5-mile run."
What Makes It Different from Just Saying "Start"?

The word "start" is neutral and plain. "Kick off" does the same job but adds a layer of:

  • Energy — something is being launched with force and intention.
  • Ceremony — it often implies that this beginning is a notable moment.
  • Forward momentum — once something kicks off, things are in motion.

Compare:

"The project started on Monday." — plain, informational.
"The project kicked off on Monday." — feels more dynamic, like it launched with purpose.

1. Don't confuse the verb and noun forms:

  • ❌ "The kickoff will kick-off at 9." (redundant — pick one)
  • ✅ "The kickoff is at 9." or "Things kick off at 9."

2. Don't use it for very small, trivial beginnings:

  • It sounds slightly odd to say "I kicked off eating my sandwich." People don't typically use it for tiny, private, instant actions.
  • It works best when there's an event, a process, or something that unfolds over time.

3. Don't separate it incorrectly with a pronoun:
When the object is a pronoun (it, them, this), it must go in the middle — never after "off."

  • ✅ "Let's kick it off!"
  • ❌ "Let's kick off it."

Knowing the family of related expressions will help you understand the full picture:

  • "Get the ball rolling" — to start something and create momentum (also a sports metaphor).
  • "Kick-start something" — to start something that needs a strong push to get going (from motorcycle engines).
  • "Launch something" — more formal, often used for products, campaigns, or events.
  • "Open" — formal, used for ceremonies ("the Mayor opened the new library").
  • "Get underway" — to begin, often used for events or journeys.
